newsitem.title: UK: UK housing bodies plead for budget leniency.
newsitem.headline: UK housing bodies plead for budget leniency.

text.p: A host of British housing bodies made last-minute pleas for leniency from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Wednesday.
Brown will deliver his first budget, and Labour's first since 1978, from 1430 GMT and is being exhorted not to choke off the recent recovery in house prices.
Overnight, Halifax Plc, Britain's newest bank and largest mortgage lender, said house prices rose 0.3 percent in June, leaving them 7.1 percent higher than a year ago.

"The June figure supports our view that the housing market in general is continuing to recover slowly and not at the pace that some commentators would suggest," the Halifax said, adding that there was no case for budget measures to rein in the market.

Brown is hotly tipped to reduce or even abolish tax relief on mortgage interest payments (MIRAS). Currently available on the first 30,000 pounds of a mortgage, the removal of that tax break would cost homeowners up to about 30 pounds per month.
The Chancellor could also raise stamp duty, currently levied at one percent of the price of a house purchase.

The Nationwide Building Society echoed the Halifax's plea. On Friday, it said house prices were up a hefty 11 percent year-on-year but its head of research, Paul Sanderson, said: "The recovery, in its early stages in many parts of the country, could still be undermined." The Nationwide said there was barely any increase in the number of transactions across the country, belying the apparent strength of prices.

One option open to Brown would be to introduce a higher rate of stamp duty on more expensive properties. That would have the effect of cooling the market where it is rising fastest -- in London and the south east, where properties are most expensive -- while leaving more subdued areas of the country untouched.
But the Council of Mortgage Lenders said on Tuesday that even in London, average prices remain well below their 1980s peak.

"Just as we thought the housing market was moving steadily towards greater health and stability, the prospect of potentially damaging budget measures has emerged," said Michael Coogan, director-general of the CML.
"Raising stamp duty or cutting mortgage interest tax relief could send waves through the market which would reverberate for a long time to come."

Not to be outdone, the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said MIRAS should be phased out over five or six years, not immediately. "For many people, particularly those on low incomes, 28 pounds per month is a significant sum," it said in its budget submission.

It too said any talk of a housing boom was overdone and only in London and the south east were prices rising significantly. "The increase in prices over the last year has been as low as 1.8 percent in the North and 1.9 percent in Scotland. There is no national housing boom."

The RICs also recoiled from a stamp duty increase, saying a one percent increase would lower house prices by between one and five percent. "Other consequences would be a fall in transactions, lower labour mobility and a rise in unemployment," it said.
